plain: In the 1950s two men, Silas Newton and Leo GeBauer, were tried for fraud over a gadget called a doodlebug, and some researchers say they were set up and treated unfairly. The two men are linked to the story of a flying saucer said to have crashed near Aztec, New Mexico. A researcher who goes by UAPGerb tells Michels about it, praising William Steinman's book on the Aztec case. He says Steinman went to Colorado and went through the court records, and found that Newton and GeBauer "were unfairly attacked in their court case." Scott Ramsey, a researcher of the Aztec crash, tells it in a later episode with more detail. He puts the trial in Denver in 1953, names a man called Herman Flader as part of the story, and says the case went through seven judges, each of whom refused it: "No, I'm not going to hear this case." Both men are summarising the records and the books rather than speaking from their own memory. If they are right, the fraud case was used to discredit two men who had spoken about a crashed saucer.
